# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is the most careful document in the series. It does what the earlier ones should have done with their open questions: registered tests before the outcomes were known, added a stricter hours measure, a controlled long-run estimate, and direct, proportionate responses to both the re-analysis and the meta-analysis. The arithmetic checks out:

- 0.966/0.88 gives +9.8% per timesheet hour, and 0.966/0.89 gives +8.5% per logged hour.
- The Halden subset: 96.8/0.866 gives +11.8%.
- The meetings difference-in-differences (−3.5 versus −0.2 hours) matches the month-six gap of 3.3 hours.
- The mediation shares sum to 100%.

The problems that remain are real but narrower. The most important is one the paper reports without drawing the consequence.

## 1. The control group changed, which affects the decay estimate

In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their meetings and raised output per hour by 4.1%. That improves the control group's mean by roughly 1.2 points (2/7 × 4.1). Part of the fall from 12.5% to 9.8% may therefore reflect controls improving rather than the treatment effect fading. That could be up to about half of the 2.7-point decline.

The paper uses this observation only to argue that reorganisation might work without cutting hours. It should also:

- Re-estimate the 24-month effect excluding those two offices, or excluding their post-month-15 data, as a sensitivity check.
- State that the 24-month estimate is the effect relative to a control group that partly adopted the proposed mechanism.
- Ask whether other control offices made smaller, unrecorded changes once a trial was visibly under way.

## 2. The decline itself isn't established

Section 3 is suitably cautious: "consistent with some fading." Section 5 states it as fact: "the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter." The two confidence intervals overlap heavily (+6.9 to +18.4 versus +4.6 to +15.2), and the paper reports no test of the within-trial change. Combined with point 1, the honest summary is that the gain may have declined somewhat and has clearly not disappeared.

This matters for symmetry. The paper rightly says the meta-analysis can't conclude there is no decay. By the same standard, this paper hasn't yet shown that decay occurred.

## 3. What do system logs actually measure?

Log-in time is described as "the stricter measure," but its scope is not the same as timesheets. It captures unclaimed work on the case system. It probably misses work done outside that system: meetings, phone calls, paperwork, training.

That has two consequences:

- **It is not clearly stricter.** It may be stricter in one direction and looser in another. If treated staff shifted their time toward system work, for example because meetings were cut, logs would understate the hours reduction relative to timesheets for compositional reasons rather than because they capture hidden work.
- **It complicates the mediation result.** If meeting time isn't in the log denominator, cutting meetings can't raise output per logged hour by shrinking the denominator. It could only do so by freeing time that then appears as more efficient case work. That is plausible, but the paper should state which mechanism it means. If meetings *are* logged, part of the mediation is close to an identity: removing hours that produce no cases raises output per hour by definition.

Either way, the paper should say whether meetings fall inside the log measure.

## 4. Mediation: "confirms" is too strong

The registration is genuine and well timed (month 11, before the 24-month outcomes). Remaining caveats:

- **The causal assumptions are not just a formality.** The Limitations section notes them, but they deserve emphasis. Offices whose managers cut meetings most may differ in managerial quality generally, which would inflate the meetings share. "Supports" would be more accurate than "confirms" in the Summary.
- **Effective sample size.** "A larger sample of office-months" is still only 14 clusters, and only 7 of them treated, which is where the mediator varies. A CI of 28 to 66% seems tight for that. The paper should state whether standard errors were bootstrapped at the office level.
- **Overlap with the data that generated the hypothesis.** If the outcome window includes months 1–9, part of the confirmatory data overlaps the period that generated the hypothesis. A test restricted to months 10–24 would be cleaner.
- **Source of the baseline meeting data.** The nine-month report had calendar data for month six only. The baseline of 7.4 hours presumably comes from retrospective calendar extraction. Saying so would resolve the concern raised about the earlier analysis.

## 5. Halden subset

- **Non-response.** Only 14 of 23 organisations agreed to take part. Organisations that reverted or struggled may be less likely to respond, so the reversion rate of 3 in 14 may understate the true rate. The paper should report what is known about the nine non-responders.
- **Hours baseline.** The baseline of 40.3 hours matches Varga & Holm's 27-organisation time-tracking figure. Is it the baseline for *these* 11 organisations? Their 17-organisation subset had 40.4. The per-hour figure depends on it.
- **The marketing agency reverted over client deadlines.** That is not a coverage problem, and the Summary's phrase "client-facing or coverage obligations" smooths over it. It is a reversion in a discretionary sector, and it suggests the two-way work-type classification misses something, such as externally imposed deadlines or responsiveness to clients. That is worth saying plainly, since the meta-analysis's own Limitations section flagged the same concern.
- **"Upper bound"** is reasonable given that the organisations are survivors twice over. Strictly, it holds only if every bias runs upward, which is likely but not guaranteed.

## 6. Questions still not reported

- **Backlog and time-to-decision.** Output per employee in case processing is now −3.4% and has been below control for two years. A persistent shortfall means a growing backlog relative to control. The case system can report backlog size, processing time and statutory deadline breaches directly. After two years these are among the most policy-relevant outcomes, and they are still missing.
- **Cost.** The counter arm got a cost estimate (+9% per contact). Case processing, with about 3 hours of overtime per week at the nine-month point, did not.
- **Quality** is still reported as raw levels (3.2% versus 3.0%) rather than as difference-in-differences with confidence intervals.

## 7. Authorship and the original working paper

The authors include the original Varden team and the Halden working paper's lead author. They are evaluating follow-ups to their own work and adjudicating critiques of it. That is common and not disqualifying, but a conflict-of-interest statement and public release of the analysis code and data would strengthen it.

More specifically, Varga & Holm showed that the Halden paper misdescribed its attrition: withdrawals happened after the pilot started, mostly for output reasons, not "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." Okafor is a co-author here, and the document cites the re-analysis, yet does not acknowledge or correct that misstatement. It should.

## On the earlier claims (§5)

Both responses are fair and proportionate:

- **The re-analysis.** "Right about the measurement problems … its conclusion that nothing remains … is not supported" is accurate. The paper meets the re-analysis's own recommended standards and still finds a gain.
- **The meta-analysis.** Confirming that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours shows the "no decay" claim was confounded, as suspected. As point 2 notes, the reply then needs the same restraint about the decline it reports.

## Where the series ends up

| Question | Best current answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain in discretionary work | Roughly 8–10%, persisting at two years; the size of any decline is uncertain and confounded by control-group changes |
| Per-worker output, discretionary | Slightly below control (−2 to −4%); backlog consequences unreported |
| Coverage-bound work | Per-worker output and service fall; the one controlled arm was ended over waiting times and cost |
| Sector-general? | No; and "discretionary" may need splitting by deadline and client exposure |
| Entirely an artifact? | No |
| Mechanism | Removing low-value meeting time likely matters more than rest. Causal shares remain uncertain, and whether reorganisation without an hours cut would capture the gain is untested |

That last question, whether the hours cut causes the gain or only forces a reorganisation that could happen anyway, is the one the paper correctly leaves open. Answering it needs a third arm that reorganises without reducing hours. That is the design to recommend next.
